A \emph{\Polya{} frequency density} is a probability density $\phi$ on $\RR$ whose translation kernel $(x, y) \mapsto \phi(x - y)$ is totally positive: every determinant $\det[\phi(x_i - y_j)]_{i,j \le n}$ with $x_1 < \dots < x_n$ and $y_1 < \dots < y_n$ is nonnegative [\sscite{karlin1968total}]. Convolution with such a density is \emph{variation-diminishing}: it does not increase the number of sign changes of a function. This is the property that the counting statements use. The selection module shows that the families of the exponents below have \Polya{} frequency kernels, and counts what they create from a signal, in its Proposition~4.5(1)--(2), p.~35.

A step of the \Matern{} pyramid in $\RR^d$ has a transform $e^{-f(|\omega|^2)}$, and Section~\ref{ch:matern} says which class the function $f$ falls in (Proposition~\ref{prop:matern-increments}). This subsection fixes the three classes it uses. A function $f : (0,\infty) \to \RR$ is \emph{completely monotone} if it is smooth and $(-1)^nf^{(n)} \ge 0$ for every $n \ge 0$. A \emph{Bernstein function} is a function $f \ge 0$ on $(0,\infty)$ whose derivative is completely monotone. These are exactly the functions \[ f(\lambda) = a + b\lambda + \int_{(0,\infty)}(1 - e^{-\lambda t})\,\eta(dt), \qquad a, b \ge 0, \quad \int_{(0,\infty)}\min(1, t)\,\eta(dt) < \infty, \] and the triplet $(a, b, \eta)$ is determined by $f$ [\sscite{schilling2012bernstein}, Thm.~3.2, p.~21]. The measure $\eta$ is the \emph{\Levy{} measure} of $f$.
A completely monotone function is a Laplace transform, by Bernstein's theorem [\sscite{schilling2012bernstein}, Thm.~1.4, p.~3].

A continuous function $\psi$ on $\RR^d$ is \emph{negative definite} when $e^{-t\psi}$ is positive definite for every $t > 0$. By [\sscite{schilling2012bernstein}, Thm.~13.14, p.~212], in the direction proved by Example~13.13 on the same page, a Bernstein function of $|\omega|^2$ is negative definite. The infinite divisibility of the law comes from subordination: Brownian motion run at the random time of a subordinator, an increasing \Levy{} process [\sscite{sato1999levy}, Thm.~30.1, pp.~197--198].

Under one dilation the decomposition is required at the one factor $c = 1/q$ only, and Sato calls the ratio $q$ a \emph{span}. Maejima and Naito require the remainder, the \emph{residual}, to be infinitely divisible [\sscite{maejima1998semi}, Def.~3.1, p.~19]. Theirs is the semi-selfdecomposable class of Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable}: $\widehat\mu = \widehat\mu(q^{-1}\,\cdot)\,\widehat\varrho_q$ for some infinitely divisible law $\varrho_q$. In a pyramid the residual is a dilate of an octave step, and every step is infinitely divisible, so the requirement costs nothing there. Without it the class is wider, and Section~\ref{sec:pyramid-bounded} shows a law of the wider class, the cubic B-spline, that is the kernel of no family.

The cubic B-spline shows why Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable} requires the residual to be infinitely divisible. With any residual the class is wider. Maejima and Naito give it Lo\`eve's name, $b$-decomposable, and note that its laws need not be infinitely divisible [\sscite{maejima1998semi}, Rem.~3.1, p.~19]. The B-spline is $b$-decomposable with $b = 2$. By $D_2\mu_1 = \mu_1 * w$ it is the law of $\tfrac12X + Y$, with $X$ of that law and $Y$ of the law $D_{1/2}w$, independent of $X$. Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable} excludes it. The B-spline has bounded support and is not a point mass, so it is not infinitely divisible (Proposition~\ref{prop:no-bounded-step}), while a semi-selfdecomposable law is (Theorem~\ref{thm:cited-A43}). Section~\ref{sec:price-masks} reads the same example on a grid, after Proposition~\ref{prop:exact-masks}.

Semi-selfdecomposability is meant in the sense of Maejima and Naito [\sscite{maejima1998semi}] (Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable}). On the line a symmetric law $\mu$ is semi-selfdecomposable with span $q > 1$ when $\widehat\mu(\omega) = \widehat\mu(\omega/q)\,\widehat\varrho_q(\omega)$ for some infinitely divisible law $\varrho_q$, the residual (Definition~\ref{def:self-decomposable} at $d = 1$). Sato's criteria for semi-selfdecomposability are recalled in Section~\ref{sec:pyramid-strata}, and folded data give a short test. For a symmetric law with folded data $(a, \varpi)$ the criterion $T_q\nu \ge \nu$ of Theorem~\ref{thm:cited-A44} reads $T_q\varpi \ge \varpi$. This holds because folding commutes with $T_q$ and a symmetric measure is determined by its fold.

The octave step is the law $L_r$ with transform $(1 + r^2|\omega|^2)^{-1}$, at $r = ct$. The literature knows it under several names, and they all denote this one law. Its density is $r^{-d}G_2(x/r)$, with $G_2$ the Bessel potential of order $2$, the kernel of $(I - \Delta)^{-1}$ [\sscite{stein1970singular}, Ch.~V, \S 3.1, (26) and Prop.~2, p.~132], read in this paper's convention for the transform. So $L_r$ is the Green's function of $I - r^2\Delta$. It is also the \Matern{} law of index $1$ at range $r$. The laws with transform $(1 + r^2|\omega|^2)^{-\gamma}$ are named after the \Matern{} covariances of spatial statistics [\sscite{whittle1954stationary}; \sscite{lindgren2011explicit}, (2)], and for $\gamma > d/2$ their densities are those covariances (Section~\ref{ch:price}). In the plane the profile is a modified Bessel function [\sscite{dlmf2026}], $b_2(y) = 2yK_1(y)$. The next lemma gives this form in every dimension. It also proves the facts on $K_0$ that two later proofs use: the limit profile in the plane, and the value of the density at its centre (Propositions~\ref{prop:thorin-in-dimension-d} and~\ref{prop:matern-generator-octave}).

One structure does carry to every dimension and every $q$. It is the mixing law of $V_t$ in Theorem~\ref{thm:matern-pyramid}(1). A \emph{generalized gamma convolution} is a weak limit of finite convolutions of gamma laws [\sscite{bondesson1992generalized}, \S 3.1, p.~30]. The variable $V_t = \sum_ic^2q^{-2i}t^2X_i$ is an almost surely convergent sum of independent exponential variables, so its law is one. The kernel $\mu_t$ is the Gaussian mixed over that law, in every dimension. No class property of $\mu_t$ itself in $\RR^d$ is claimed.

For laws the bijection is a known construction. Maejima and Sato build the semi-selfsimilar additive processes from paths of laws over one period with these conditions [\sscite{maejima1999semi}, Thm.~7, p.~361]. What this section adds is the reading in the scale-space axioms and what follows from it.
